lesson.title: Derivatives: Measuring Instantaneous Rate of Change
lesson.summary: A derivative is defined as the limit of a difference quotient, giving the slope of a curve at a single instant rather than the constant slope between two far-apart points, extending the idea of slope from linear equations to curves that bend.
lesson.body:
In the linear equations chapter, slope was simple because a line never changes direction: the rise over run between any two points on that line always gives the same number. A curve like f(x) equals x squared has no such luxury. Its steepness is different at every single point, gentle near x = 0 and increasingly steep as x grows, so a single slope value cannot describe the whole curve. What is needed instead is a way to measure the slope at one specific point, an instantaneous rate of change, and that is precisely what a derivative provides, using the limit concept from the previous chapter to make the idea precise.

Start with two points on a curve, x and a nearby point x plus h, where h is some small number representing the gap between them. The slope of the straight line connecting those two points, called a secant line, is the familiar rise over run: [f(x plus h) minus f(x)] divided by h. This expression is called the difference quotient. As h shrinks closer and closer to 0, the second point slides in toward the first, and the secant line rotates until it becomes the tangent line, the line that just grazes the curve at that single point. The derivative, written f prime of x, is defined as the limit of the difference quotient as h approaches 0: f prime of x equals the limit as h approaches 0 of [f(x plus h) minus f(x)] divided by h. This is exactly a limit in the sense of the previous chapter, since plugging h = 0 directly would give 0 divided by 0, an undefined expression, just as the earlier limit example did.

Apply this to f(x) equals x squared. Compute the difference quotient: f(x plus h) is (x plus h) squared, which expands to x squared plus 2xh plus h squared. Subtracting f(x), which is x squared, leaves 2xh plus h squared. Dividing by h gives 2x plus h. Now take the limit as h approaches 0: the h term simply vanishes, since it is being driven to 0, leaving the derivative f prime of x equals 2x. At x = 3, that means f prime of 3 equals 2 times 3, which is 6. You can sanity check this numerically the same way limits were checked earlier: using a very small h of 0.001, f(3.001) equals 3.001 squared, which is 9.006001, and f(3) is 9, so the difference quotient is 0.006001 divided by 0.001, which is 6.001, extremely close to the predicted value of 6.

The number 6 here means something concrete: at the exact point x = 3 on the curve y = x squared, the tangent line touching the curve has a slope of 6, the same kind of slope you calculated directly for a straight line back in the linear equations chapter. The difference now is that the slope itself is a function of x, changing from point to point along the curve, which is exactly what f prime of x equals 2x expresses: a rule that hands back the correct instantaneous slope for whatever x value you plug in.
